status: provisional planning model (October 20, 2026). Every number below is an ASSUMPTION about how long a competent player needs for a Minecraft task. Nobody has timed a person. scripts/economy_model.py reads this file and the real game data (work orders, exchange prices, recipes, properties) and prints what the data implies; replace these numbers with measurements from a played session and the whole model updates.
active_minute: one minute with at least one human online; the clock of work-order demand, exchange restocking and rent (D-012, D-099)

overhead.note: Accepting and delivering are two terminal interactions with a short walk; a trip to a city exchange is a round trip of about twelve minutes between a home near Founders Row and a city terminal (docs/design/cities-and-world.md: 6-8 minutes one way), shared by the orders one trip's purchases cover.

hands_on_minutes_each.note: Hands-on minutes to obtain ONE of the item from the world with starter tools, including crafting it. Waiting (crops, smelting) is parallel and listed separately in wait_minutes. Workshop goods (D-163) count their inputs at these rates plus a little handling at the station; the station's own time is waiting.

wait_minutes.note: Latency before the FIRST delivery of an order that needs growing or ageing; later cycles overlap with other work.

gun_minutes.note: A gun costs its recipe's iron-equivalent value (contracts.json reference_values.guns); gathering that iron takes minutes_per_iron per ingot, assembly at the Gun Smith Table bench_minutes.

starting_state.note: A new citizen starts with the starter kit and no credits (RegistrationService). The motel's first two billing cycles are a welcome gift of the city (D-099).

targets.note: Provisional targets from the owner's brief (section 3.2 and 4.3), tuned against the model, not hard-coded game rules.

efficiency.note: Only about half of an active hour is hands-on production: the rest is walking to a terminal, finding things, inventory, waiting for a furnace, talking to a friend. A 30 minute session is roughly 5 minutes of setting up, 8 of travel and trading and 17 of work. Every income figure is multiplied by this; rent, upkeep and living costs are not.

living_costs.note: Torches, food and water bought on the road (wayside desk prices in survival-supply.json) for a player who eats and drinks mostly from their own farm and wells.

courier_orders.note: Errands that carry exchange goods to a buyer unchanged. They pay a courier's margin (not a crafter's) and are bounded by the shelf: the exchange restocks a few units an hour for everyone, so the profit per hour is capped no matter how fast the player walks. The underground errands also carry the seizure risk of contraband (D-052). The cap compares the errand's net credits per hour (the smaller of what the shelf and the employer allow, times its margin) with the best crafting careers' 400-480: a courier is never the best hour.

scarcity.note: A new world made with the scarcity package (D-120) has no ore to mine: every unit of iron, copper, coal or redstone in what an order asks for comes off a city's finite shelf (bought) or, for the base metals, out of the regrowing quarry (D-123). ore_content is the ore-derived content of the vanilla goods the work orders ask for, from the base-game recipes; the mining time the default model counts for those units is taken out and replaced by the shelf price (and an exchange run) or by quarry_minutes_each. Provisional, like every hands-on minute. Nether quartz (comparators, observers, daylight detectors) is mined in no world here: it is counted as a shelf good in the scarcity model (D-175), while the ore-world model keeps its provisional hands-on minutes.

station_tiers.source: ASSUMPTION for scripts/career_balance.py: the tier a career's workshop stations are fitted to by level. A tier is fitted from real parts the career makes (WorkshopBlock.upgrade; tier 3 needs the station's skill), a few hundred credits of parts, affordable by the levels named (the affordability table). Graded goods pay by grade (Workshops.GRADE_PRICE), so a character who never upgrades earns less than this.

service_work.status: Service calls of the Technician (TechService, TechWork) and the Smith (MachineService, SmithWork) for scripts/career_balance.py. Fees, gaps, skill reach and the parts a job uses are CODE (tests/test_career_balance.py reads them from the Java); the minutes a job takes and the tier of the building it is at are ASSUMPTIONS.
service_work.building_tier_source: Assumption: the mean tier of the lockable buildings a call comes from (PropertyIntel's neighbourhood grades spread tiers II to VI, docs/technical/property-intelligence.md); a call is at one of the panels or drives nearest a player in the city.

jobs.source: TechService.repairFee and repairXp; a new fault every 8 to 15 minutes in a city somebody is in (FAULT_GAP_MIN/MAX: 5.2 an hour), two open at most; a tier III or higher repair uses a circuit board (TechWork.succeed). Minutes: a walk to a panel near you and the trace puzzle (120 s at most); tech run 5 took about five.

TechService.installFee and installXp (D-210); two installs open in a city and topped up as they are taken (MAX_INSTALLS); the job uses a Municipal Security Array. Minutes: a walk and the patch puzzle (180 s at most). The rate is an assumption of how many a player finds near them.
TechService.upgradeFee (D-210) and upgradeXp; one open in a city (MAX_UPGRADES), at an office, industrial or commercial building of tier III or higher; wears a repair kit. The rate is an assumption.

MachineService.fee and xp; a breakdown every 10 to 16 minutes (GAP_MIN/MAX: 4.6 an hour), two open at most; the drive's worn parts are replaced with the Smith's own (SmithPuzzles.Kind: a coupling's bracket, a bearing set, a gear set or springs; two is typical). Minutes: a walk to the drive and the drive puzzle; engineer run 7 took about seven.

police_risk.status: ASSUMPTIONS for scripts/career_balance.py (twelfth pass). The odds of being noticed are estimates built from code-defined chances (named in each source); the chance of an arrest once noticed is a placeholder until the scripted police runs of the twelfth pass give an observed rate (docs/technical/career-balance.md says which numbers are measured).
police_risk.p_arrest_source: Assumption. Officers run at about 5.0 blocks a second against a walking 4.3 and a sprinting 5.6 (PoliceResponse.CHASE_SPEED, PoliceChaseGameTests), chase only what they see and give up 30 s out of sight (PoliceResponse.GIVE_UP_SECONDS); a thief who is noticed but runs at once and breaks the line of sight gets away more often than not. To be replaced by the arrest share of the scripted police runs.

raid.source: The bonded store (D-173) is a high-security warehouse: its class's alarm is certain unless a Technician's back channel quietens it (TechService.quieted), its cameras are Core's, a patrol walks outside. 0.6 assumes the job is prepared (the line quietened, the cameras looped) and still often goes wrong; the fine is Ironhaven's theft (city_laws/ironhaven.json).

burglary.source: Minutes: casing, a lock, five searches and the way out (the Thief scenario took 9 to 16 minutes per house; burglary_audit.py's TYPICAL house), and a fence trip shared by three visits. Noticed: the class's alarm chance (building_security/classes.json: 0.25 at tier 2 to certain at tier 6) for a pick that is not clean (a clean pick slips an alarm below 0.9, PoliceResponse.QUIET_BYPASS_MAX_CHANCE), plus a witness in the street (the city's witness chance, 0.2 to 0.35, with somebody in sight about two times in five), a household at home hearing a search (CrimeWatch.searched: 0.3 by day) and a patrol in sight. The fine is a break-in's or a theft's (80 to 110 by city). The tier a thief works rises with experience (tier_by_level, an assumption). Lockpicks are crafted from two iron nuggets and a stick. The fence pays at most about 390 credits an hour after its opening budget (economy-model.md, the fence table).
